title: Clothes and Status
objective: After this level you can describe medieval clothes and what they said about status.
summary: Wool clothed almost everyone, from cheap russet to costly scarlet. England’s 1363 law set what each rank could wear, and a 1463 law capped pointed shoes, whose fashion shows up in medieval bones.

cards.headline: Your medieval neighbours could read your rank from across the street.
cards.body: No ID card needed: the cloth on your back did the talking. It talked so loudly that the law stepped in.

cards.headline: Wool for everyone, but not the same wool
cards.body: In 14th-century England, wool was the fabric people bought most, and linen came second. But “wool” covered a huge range, from cheap, coarse russet and blanket to costly scarlet. Two people could both wear wool and still look worlds apart, the way a cheap T-shirt and a designer one are both cotton.

cards.headline: Dressing by law
cards.body: In 1363 England passed a law setting what cloth each rank could wear, from servants and craftsmen up to merchants and knights. It blamed the “outrageous and excessive apparel” of people dressing above their “estate and degree”. The lowest ranks were limited to blanket and russet worth no more than 12 pence. Did it work? Laws like this have proved difficult or impossible to enforce over the long term.

cards.headline: The pointy-shoe problem
cards.body: Late-medieval fashion loved poulaines, shoes with long pointed toes. In 1463 King Edward IV limited the points in London to under two inches. The fashion left marks you can still measure: Cambridge researchers found bunions in 6% of people buried in the 11th to 13th centuries, but 27% of those buried in the 14th and 15th. The bones kept the receipts.

Pointed shoes left their mark in medieval bones

questions.prompt: What did England’s law of 1363 on apparel try to control?

options.label: The price of wool sold abroad
options.rationale: It looked at who wore what.

options.label: What cloth people of each rank could wear
Which colours knights painted on shields
How many shoes a family could own

questions.explanation: The 1363 law set what cloth each rank could wear, blaming people who dressed above their “estate and degree”.

questions.prompt: Why do Cambridge researchers link a rise in medieval bunions to fashion?

options.label: Bunions rose as pointed shoes came into style
Bunions appeared only among farm workers
options.rationale: They were more common among the wealthy.

options.label: Wool clothing rubbed people’s feet
options.rationale: The link was to shoes, not cloth.

options.label: A law forced everyone to wear tight boots

questions.explanation: Bunions rose from 6% of burials in the 11th to 13th centuries to 27% in the 14th and 15th, as pointed poulaines spread.

questions.prompt: Level 54’s bread came in fine and rough grades by rank. Which cloth did the 1363 law leave to the lowest ranks?

options.label: Silk and fur
options.rationale: Those were for the highest ranks.

options.label: Costly scarlet wool
options.rationale: Scarlet was among the dearest cloths.

options.label: Cloth of gold
options.rationale: That was reserved for the very top.

questions.explanation: Like rough loaves for servants, cheap blanket and russet, worth no more than 12 pence, were for the lowest ranks.
